title: Square a crooked cabinet door by turning its lower cup hinge's side screw with a PH2 screwdriver until the gap is even
instruction: The right-hand cabinet door hangs crooked, so the gap between the two doors is uneven. Make the gap even, 2 to 3 mm wide from top to bottom, and leave the door shut.
context: Hanging and squaring cabinet doors is part of installing cabinets, regular work for carpenters (889,700 US jobs in 2025) and for maintenance and repair workers who adjust fixtures with hand tools. A cup hinge's side screw moves the door only while the screwdriver sits square in its recess and is pushed as it turns; tilted or pushed too lightly, it slips out (cam-out) and the door stays crooked.
setup: Centimetres; x forward from the line through the arm bases, y to the robot's left, heights above the bench. A painted wall section (1.25 thick, 88 wide, 62 tall) stands fixed at x 72 to 73.25, y -32 to 56. On it hang two frameless wall cabinets of 1.8 cm white melamine-faced particleboard (0.8 back), 30 deep (fronts at x 42), 40 tall (undersides 3 above the bench): ours 45 wide (y -25 to 20) and its neighbour 30 wide (y 20 to 50). The neighbour's door (grey melamine-faced particleboard, 29.7 wide, 39.6 tall, 1.9 thick) is shut and square, its right-hand edge at y 20.12, with a 3.2 cm black metal knob (2.7 proud) 3.5 in from that edge and 6 up. Our door (same material, 44.6 wide, 39.6 tall, 1.9 thick, 2.2 kg, same knob 3.5 in from its free left-hand edge) hangs on two Blum CLIP top 110-degree spring hinges (71T3550; 35 mm cups 2.25 from the hinge edge, 8 from the door's top and bottom) clipped to 0 mm mounting plates on the inside of our right-hand side panel, centred 3.7 behind its front edge. It stands open 50 degrees. Shut, it is crooked: the gap to the neighbour's door is 0.16 at 2 above the bottom and 0.28 at 2 below the top, because the lower hinge sits 0.7 mm too far towards the free edge. Each hinge arm has a side-adjustment screw (PH2 cross recess, 9 mm head, 2.4 behind the cabinet's front, its face 1.6 out from the side panel; found at mid-travel, a paint mark on its head) and a depth screw 5.2 behind the front. A PH2 screwdriver (SimReady prop, 18.8 long, 3.4 handle, 0.10 kg) stands tip down in a pine stand (7 x 7 x 4.5, fixed to the bench, stepped bore 0.56 then 1.06 wide) centred at x 24, y 24. Distractors, loose on the bench, ignored by the scoring: a ceramic mug (11.4 x 9 x 8, 0.30 kg) at x 28, y -37; a closed retractable utility knife (16 x 6.1 x 2.6, 0.15 kg) at x 12, y -28; a thin marker pen (10.9 long, 0.01 kg) at x 12, y 25.
scoring: Gaps: between the two doors' facing edges at 2 cm below the top and 2 cm above the bottom (feeler gauges in 0.1 mm steps). Shut: our door within 0.5 degrees of its closed stop. Clear: every fingertip of both grippers at least 3 cm from both doors and both cabinets (with the hinges inside). Still: the door's free edge moving under 9 mm/s. 1.0: shut, both gaps 2.0 to 3.0 mm and within 0.5 mm of each other, clear and still, all held for 1 s. 0.5: at the end, shut with gaps in that window, without the 1.0 conditions held for 1 s (not clear, not still, or not yet for 1 s). 0.25: otherwise, at the end the lower hinge's side screw has turned at least a quarter turn clockwise (the way that opens the bottom gap) from where it was found (its paint mark). 0: anything else. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Turn the lower side screw back to its paint mark (the gaps return to 1.6 and 2.8 mm), put the screwdriver back in its stand and open the door to 50 degrees against a tape mark.
fidelity: Rigid primitive cabinets, doors and hinge parts. The hinges are modelled by their working: a swing joint spring-shut below 25 degrees (estimate), and side screws that move the door 1 mm per turn (assumed), +-2 mm to a stop. The PH2 recess is a sprung funnel; the screw turns only with the tip seated within 0.8 mm, the driver within 6 degrees and pushed with at least 10 N, against 0.2 N m (estimates). Depth screws fixed; door gravity off. SimReady screwdriver, mesh (SDF) collision.
